items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: and eventually Duke Ellington in the late 30s

ctx.x: Yes certainly it was before LPs, but the idea of him spreading through recording.

Well that’s absolutely true, because people got to know the history of jazz that way, through LPs even more than those 78s that I just talked about, that started around 1940. And the fact that it was an organized series meant that people knew that they could expect another release the following month, and that way they were on the lookout. And the annotations that I wrote for the 78 RPM albums were the first group of written documentation of the careers of some of these performers, because before that there…

rather special reason that I didn’t catch on to at first, which was that the American jazz records that got released abroad tended to stay in the catalogues. They didn’t sell very widely and the record business was smaller in Europe than it was in America, and because they stayed in the catalogues they were there for reference as more and more people got interested in the historical recordings of the 1920s and early 30s. In America they got cut out rather quickly because there was so much of an emphasis on the…

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: that was what Duke and I talked about as the centerpiece of the performance, that this would be a historic moment, the first time anyone had recorded at a music festival of any kind

ctx.x: What was the most glorious moment musically?

There were certainly – maybe three. I’ll put it that way. One was absolutely listening to the Duke Ellington band at Newport playing Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue, which was a very surprise thing. I’ve written about it in the liner notes. So I’ll just say very briefly that this was not expected on the program. Duke threw it in at the last minute. Paul Gonsalves didn’t remember that he had played it once before, and he was of course the centerpiece of the whole thing. He blew into the wrong microphone, after I…

because apparently the band was pretty tight about the difficulty of the composition, which was not an easy composition. That’s when he said, “Let’s play something we haven’t played in a long time. Let’s play Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue.” That’s when Paul said, “But I don’t know the piece.” Duke said, “You’ve got the solo on this.” “What?” Yeah, “We’ll just bring you in for the key change, and I’ll take you out. That’s it. You just keep blowing the blues in between.” Another fantastic moment was after I had…
